claims.text: The nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform, single-phase atomic distribution.
In situ high-resolution STEM with a specialized heating stage can investigate the thermal behavior of these nanoparticles at atomic scale.
Atomic-scale images and elemental maps can be acquired simultaneously during progressive heating.
The proposed experiment spans room temperature to approximately 700–900 °C.
During initial heating, the nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous, nearly equiatomic atomic structure.
Above a high-temperature threshold, atomic-scale rearrangements will occur.
High-temperature rearrangements will produce local elemental segregation and phase evolution.
Atomic-scale structural reconfiguration and elemental redistribution mediate the response to heating.
At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy maintains a uniform elemental distribution.
Increasing temperature causes differences in atomic mobility and thermodynamic driving forces to promote localized segregation.
Thermodynamic driving forces at elevated temperature promote phase evolution.
Atomic-scale uniformity will be maintained at moderate elevated temperatures.
At or above a critical temperature, STEM will reveal local elemental segregation and/or subtle phase transformations.
Electron-beam effects can influence the observed thermal behavior.
Nanoparticle size variation can influence the observations.
The critical segregation temperature may vary with heating rate and experimental conditions.
A room-temperature sample maintained under identical beam conditions provides a control for beam-induced changes.
Failure to observe segregation or phase evolution at high temperature relative to room temperature would falsify the proposed detectable thermal alteration.

contradictions.description: The mechanism assigns stabilization and retained uniformity to configurational entropy, whereas the falsification rule describes detectable atomic alterations as resulting from 'thermodynamic stabilization.' This reverses the stated role of stabilization.
